quote: Our primary recommendation is that healthy adults perform RT with high effort (effort can be measured through various scales, but can be achieved with various loads and sets per the FITT-VP principle) at least twice weekly, with all major muscle groups being engaged.
claim: ACSM's primary recommendation: healthy adults should do resistance training with high effort at least twice a week, covering all major muscle groups; many load and set combinations achieve this.
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: baseline weekly structure for any strength plan

quote: Between RTx, hypertrophy was enhanced by RT performed with eccentric-only contractions (versus concentric-only) and higher volume (≥10 sets/muscle group/wk).
claim: Muscle hypertrophy is enhanced by higher weekly volume, at least 10 sets per muscle group per week, and by eccentric emphasis.
number: >=10 sets per muscle group per week
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: weekly set target for hypertrophy goals

quote: voluntary strength was enhanced by lifting heavier loads (≥80% one-repetition maximum), through a complete range of motion, for 2–3 sets, at the beginning of training sessions, and ≥2 sessions/wk.
claim: Maximal strength is enhanced by heavier loads (at least 80% of one-repetition maximum), full range of motion, 2-3 sets per exercise, placing the exercise early in the session, and training at least 2 sessions per week.
number: >=80% of one-repetition maximum; 2-3 sets per exercise; >=2 sessions per week
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)

quote: A meta-regression (187) of the effect of volume (weekly) sets showed progression, but as expected, a dose-response that plateaued and showed diminishing returns beyond ~2–3 sets/exercise for strength and ~18–20 weekly sets for hypertrophy with varying loads; thus, healthy adults are advised to complete at least two sets per exercise.
claim: ACSM advises at least two sets per exercise; citing a meta-regression, it states that returns diminish beyond about 2-3 sets per exercise for strength and about 18-20 weekly sets for hypertrophy.
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: upper end of useful weekly volume
caveat: Pelland2024 found no clear hypertrophy plateau up to the volumes studied (few studies above about 25 fractional sets); the 18-20 figure is a point of diminishing returns, not a hard ceiling

quote: Completing sets to fatigue (momentary muscular failure) does not enhance gains in strength, hypertrophy, and power, and so is not necessary for benefits to occur. ... Sufficient effort (assessed using various scales) can be accomplished by completing sets with various RTx and completion of “near-failure” or a target of 2–3 repetitions in reserve (RIR)
claim: Training to momentary failure is not necessary for strength, hypertrophy or power gains; sufficient effort is reached by stopping near failure, about 2-3 repetitions in reserve.
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: default RIR target for working sets
caveat: Robinson2024 meta-regression suggests hypertrophy keeps improving as sets end closer to failure; ACSM also says evidence is insufficient to set exact RIR targets

quote: RT did not influence hypertrophy performed with low (1 d/wk) versus high (>5 d/wk) frequency when total volume was equated; low (30% 1RM) to high (100% 1RM) loads; contractions to muscle failure/fatigue; blood flow restriction; varying loads during repetitions; fast (0.5 s) versus slow (8 s) repetitions; power training techniques; periodization (linear, undulating, and nonperiodized)
claim: Hypertrophy was not influenced by frequency (1 versus more than 5 days per week at equal volume), load (30% to 100% of 1RM), training to failure, repetition tempo (0.5 s versus 8 s) or periodization model.
number: 1 vs >5 d/wk at equal volume; 30-100% 1RM; 0.5 s vs 8 s repetitions
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: freedom to choose load, tempo and split for hypertrophy; load or tempo changes when a joint is irritated

quote: Strength was not affected by RT performed with contractions to muscle failure/fatigue, free weights versus machines, unstable versus stable surfaces; fast (<2 s) versus moderate-slow (>2 s) contractions, morning versus evening training sessions, short (<1 min) versus long (>1 min) between-set rest intervals
claim: Strength gains were not affected by training to failure, free weights versus machines, tempo (<2 s versus >2 s contractions), time of day, or short (<1 min) versus long (>1 min) rest between sets.
number: <2 s vs >2 s contractions; <1 min vs >1 min rest
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: equipment choice, tempo and rest flexibility
caveat: the rest-interval finding is based mainly on untrained people; Grgic2018b suggests trained lifters need more than 2 min to maximise strength

quote: With appropriate progressive overload, periodization is not significantly superior to nonperiodized programs; thus, periodization is less important than previously hypothesized (11,12) for healthy adults to improve muscle function and hypertrophy.
claim: With appropriate progressive overload, periodized programs are not significantly better than non-periodized programs for healthy adults; periodization matters less than once thought.
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: how much to invest in periodization models
caveat: Moesgaard2022 found a small 1RM advantage for periodized and undulating programs in volume-equated studies, mainly in trained people; ACSM notes periodization for peaking is understudied

quote: Notably, as the results in Table 4 highlight, progression is not necessary to achieve beneficial outcomes, and overload, or more accurately, increasing the stimulus in some manner, is likely a requirement only for those seeking continued longer term progress.
claim: Progressive overload is not required to obtain benefits from resistance training, but increasing the stimulus in some way is likely needed for continued longer-term progress.
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)

quote: Strength is improved by RT, including circuit RT, elastic band RT, home-based RT, and velocity-based RT. ... Hypertrophy is improved by RT, including circuit RT and elastic band RT.
claim: Compared with no training, strength improves with circuit, elastic-band, home-based and velocity-based resistance training, and hypertrophy improves with circuit and elastic-band training.
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)

quote: applying the recommendations herein to the body regions “upper” and “lower” for “push” and “pull” exercises (i.e., four body regions) is sufficient to target major muscle groups
claim: In the authors' view, covering upper-body push, upper-body pull, lower-body push and lower-body pull is sufficient to train all major muscle groups (optionally splitting upper body into horizontal and vertical).
population: healthy adults >=18 y, mostly novice trainees (overview of 137 systematic reviews)
used_for: minimum exercise selection for a full-body session
caveat: expert view of the writing group, not a tested comparison

quote: In 23 studies (n = 1174) of adults with coronary heart disease, all 63 nonfatal cardiovascular complications occurred during aerobic training, and the 20 musculoskeletal complications that occurred during RT were caused by preexisting conditions (knee arthritis) and were resolved by changing RT intensity or body position
claim: In 23 studies of adults with coronary heart disease (reported by ACSM from a cited source), the 20 musculoskeletal complications during resistance training stemmed from pre-existing knee arthritis and were resolved by changing training intensity or body position.
population: adults with coronary heart disease in exercise trials (n = 1174)
used_for: programming response to joint pain: modify load or position rather than stop
caveat: clinical population; the coach still refers persistent or worsening pain (see SAF)

quote: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.
claim: When the athlete can do one to two repetitions more than the target number with the current load, increase the load by 2-10%.
caveat: expert recommendation from 2009, not tested against alternatives; use the smaller end for upper-body and small-muscle exercises

quote: eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets ... with emphasis on the 6-12 RM zone using 1- to 2-min rest periods between sets at a moderate velocity
claim: ACSM 2009 recommended 3-5 min rest between heavy sets (1-6 RM) for strength and 1-2 min rest for hypertrophy work in the 6-12 RM zone.
number: 3-5 min rest (1-6 RM); 1-2 min rest (6-12 RM)
population: intermediate to advanced healthy adults (2009 position stand; superseded)
caveat: Singer2024 found no hypertrophy benefit of short rest; resting more than about 90 s appears at least as good

quote: For novice (untrained individuals with no RT experience or who have not trained for several years) training, it is recommended that loads correspond to a repetition range of an 8-12 repetition maximum (RM). For intermediate (individuals with approximately 6 months of consistent RT experience)
claim: ACSM 2009 defines novices as people with no resistance-training experience or none for several years (recommended loads 8-12 RM) and intermediates as people with about 6 months of consistent training.
caveat: definitions are conventions, not evidence-derived thresholds

quote: The posterior probability of the marginal slope exceeding zero for the effect of volume on both hypertrophy and strength was 100%, indicating that gains in muscle size and strength increase as volume increases. However, both best-fit models suggest diminishing returns, with the diminishing returns for strength being considerably more pronounced.
claim: Gains in muscle size and strength both increase with weekly set volume, with diminishing returns that are much more pronounced for strength than for hypertrophy.
population: 67 studies, 2058 participants (79% male, mean age 25 y)
used_for: volume progression logic for hypertrophy versus strength

quote: The posterior probability of the marginal slope exceeding zero for frequency's effect on hypertrophy was less than 100%, indicating compatibility with negligible effects. In contrast, the posterior probability for strength was 100%, suggesting strength gains increase with increasing frequency, albeit with diminishing returns.
claim: At a given weekly volume, training frequency has a negligible effect on hypertrophy, whereas strength gains increase with frequency, with diminishing returns.
population: 67 studies, 2058 participants (79% male, mean age 25 y)
used_for: choosing sessions per week per muscle or lift

quote: weekly set volume/frequency for indirect sets was quantified as 1 for 'total,' 0.5 for 'fractional,' and 0 for 'direct.' ... The relative evidence for the 'fractional' quantification method was strongest
claim: When counting weekly sets per muscle, count a set that trains the muscle indirectly (for example triceps in a bench press) as half a set; this fractional method predicted outcomes best.
used_for: counting weekly sets per muscle group

quote: the minimum effective dose occurs with low volume (4 'fractional' weekly sets), the tiers also indicate no clear plateau in the primary meta-regression. Instead, they suggest an increasing number of sets needed to elicit detectable additional hypertrophy. However, caution is warranted as few studies have explored ~25+ 'fractional' weekly sets.
claim: About 4 fractional sets per muscle per week is the minimum effective dose for detectable hypertrophy; there was no clear plateau, but more and more extra sets are needed for each further detectable gain, and few studies tested more than about 25 weekly sets.
used_for: minimum and upper weekly volume for hypertrophy
caveat: preprint numbers; published version paywalled and may differ

quote: Higher Efficiency 5 - 10 ~6 additional weekly sets required for additional detectable hypertrophy Intermediate Efficiency 11 - 18 ~8.5 additional weekly sets required for additional detectable hypertrophy Lower Efficiency 19 - 29 ~10.75 additional weekly sets required for additional detectable hypertrophy
claim: Hypertrophy efficiency falls with volume: at 5-10 fractional weekly sets about 6 more sets are needed for a further detectable gain, at 11-18 about 8.5 more, and at 19-29 about 10.75 more.
used_for: deciding whether adding sets is worth the time and fatigue
caveat: preprint numbers; detectable gain threshold was 2.05% hypertrophy

quote: one set was identified as the minimum effective dose. Additional increments in the SDES were observed up to approximately 4 'fractional' weekly sets, but not beyond this point.
claim: For strength, one fractional weekly set per muscle was the minimum effective dose, and detectable extra strength gains were seen up to about 4 fractional weekly sets but not beyond.
population: 67 studies, mostly untrained or recreationally trained young adults (preprint data)
caveat: large learning effect on novel strength tests; in well-trained powerlifters 1-3 direct weekly sets were insufficient (cited in the same paper)

quote: performing a single set of 6-12 repetitions with loads ranging from approximately 70-85% 1RM 2-3 times per week with high intensity of effort (reaching volitional or momentary failure) for 8-12 weeks can produce suboptimal, yet significant increases in SQ and BP 1RM strength in resistance-trained men.
claim: In resistance-trained men, one set of 6-12 repetitions at about 70-85% 1RM taken to failure, 2-3 times per week for 8-12 weeks, produced significant but suboptimal squat and bench press 1RM gains.
number: 1 set of 6-12 reps at 70-85% 1RM, 2-3 times per week, 8-12 weeks
used_for: minimal-dose plans when time is very limited
caveat: unclear for deadlift, women and highly trained strength athletes

quote: perform a minimum of one leg pressing exercise (e.g. squats), one upper-body pulling exercise (e.g. pull-up) and one upper-body pushing exercise (e.g. bench press). ... we recommend performing a minimum of 4 weekly sets per muscle group using a 6-15 RM loading range (15-40 repetitions can be used if training is performed to volitional failure).
claim: For time-efficient training, include at least one leg press or squat pattern, one upper-body pull and one upper-body push, and do at least 4 weekly sets per muscle group at 6-15 RM (or 15-40 repetitions if sets go to failure).
number: 4 weekly sets per muscle group; 6-15 RM; 15-40 repetitions to failure
used_for: minimal effective plan for people with 2-3 short sessions per week

quote: Advanced training techniques, such as supersets, drop sets and rest-pause training roughly halves training time compared to traditional training, while maintaining training volume. However, these methods are probably better at inducing hypertrophy than muscular strength
claim: Supersets, drop sets and rest-pause sets roughly halve session time while keeping volume, but are probably better for hypertrophy than for maximal strength.

quote: the effects of low- (>15 repetitions maximum (RM)), moderate- (9-15 RM), and high-load (≤8 RM) RTs were examined in healthy adults. ... Although muscle hypertrophy improvements seem to be load independent, increases in muscle strength are superior in high-load RT programs.
claim: When sets are taken to failure, low (>15 RM), moderate (9-15 RM) and high (8 RM or heavier) loads produce similar hypertrophy, but strength gains are greater with high loads.
population: healthy adults, 28 studies, 747 participants; sets to volitional failure
used_for: load choice for hypertrophy versus strength; using lighter loads when heavy loading is not tolerated
caveat: light loads only match hypertrophy when sets are taken close to failure

quote: there is strong evidence that resistance training frequency does not significantly or meaningfully impact muscle hypertrophy when volume is equated. Thus, for a given training volume, individuals can choose a weekly frequency per muscle groups based on personal preference.
claim: At equal weekly volume, training frequency does not meaningfully affect hypertrophy, so frequency per muscle group can be chosen by preference and schedule.

quote: Strength gains were similar across a wide range of RIR, while muscle hypertrophy improves as sets are terminated closer to failure.
claim: Strength gains were similar across a wide range of repetitions in reserve, while hypertrophy improved as sets were stopped closer to failure.
population: resistance-training studies in healthy adults (exploratory meta-regressions)
used_for: RIR targets for hypertrophy versus strength
caveat: RIR was estimated from study descriptions; exploratory; ACSM2026-RT and Refalo2023 found no clear advantage of training to failure

quote: found no advantage for either resistance training performed to momentary muscular failure versus non-failure for muscle hypertrophy [effect size=0.12 (95% confidence interval -0.13, 0.37), p=0.343]
claim: Training to momentary muscular failure gave no significant hypertrophy advantage over stopping short of failure (effect size 0.12, confidence interval crossing zero).
population: healthy adults of any age and training status (15 studies)
caveat: the authors suggest a non-linear relationship: close to failure may matter, reaching failure itself may not

quote: Subjects reported an RPE value that corresponded to an RIR value (RPE-10 = 0-RIR, RPE-9 = 1-RIR, and so forth).
claim: On the RIR-based RPE scale, RPE 10 means 0 repetitions in reserve, RPE 9 means 1 in reserve, and so on (RPE 8 = 2 RIR).
used_for: translating RPE and RIR in plan tables

quote: Therefore, novice lifters should practice recording RIR, but likely not base training intensity or progression solely on the RIR-based scale until increased accuracy is achieved. A possible way to gauge this is to take a submaximal set short of failure and record a score followed by a subsequent set at the same load that is taken to failure to test if the score was accurate.
claim: Novices should record RIR but not base load or progression solely on it until their ratings are accurate; accuracy can be checked by rating a submaximal set and then taking a set with the same load to failure.
used_for: when to rely on RIR with beginners
caveat: expert opinion; testing to failure should use safe exercises (machines or with a spotter)

quote: Training at an RIR of 0 (to failure) should be ... limited to the final set performed for a given body part and primarily relegated to exercises with a low biomechanical complexity and risk of injury ... for main movements (squats, bench press, etc.) primarily performing sets within the RPE range of 6–8 (i.e., 2–4 RIR) may be an appropriate strategy
claim: For hypertrophy, keep main compound lifts mostly at RPE 6-8 (2-4 RIR) and limit sets to failure (0 RIR) to the last set for a body part on simple, low-risk isolation exercises.
number: RPE 6-8 (2-4 RIR) on main lifts; 0 RIR only on last isolation set
caveat: expert opinion

quote: participants tended to underpredict the number of repetitions to task failure by 0.95 repetitions (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.17-1.73) ... participants' training status did not seem to influence prediction accuracy
claim: People underestimate how many repetitions they have left by about 1 repetition on average, and training status does not improve this accuracy.
caveat: large heterogeneity; accuracy improves closer to failure, with heavier loads (12 or fewer repetitions) and in later sets

quote: results suggest a small hypertrophic benefit to employing inter-set rest interval durations >60 s, perhaps mediated by reductions in volume load. However, our analysis did not detect appreciable differences in hypertrophy when resting >90 s between sets
claim: Resting more than 60 s between sets gives a small hypertrophy benefit, and no appreciable difference was seen between rest periods longer than 90 s.

quote: robust gains in muscular strength can be achieved even with short RIs (< 60 s). However, it seems that longer duration RIs (> 2 min) are required to maximize strength gains in resistance-trained individuals. With regard to untrained individuals, it seems that short to moderate RIs (60-120 s) are sufficient for maximizing muscular strength gains.
claim: Strength improves even with rests under 60 s, but resistance-trained people need more than 2 min to maximise strength gains, while 60-120 s is sufficient for untrained people.
used_for: rest intervals for strength by training status
caveat: ACSM2026-RT found no effect of short versus long rest on strength, mainly in novices

quote: Both progressions of repetitions and load appear to be viable strategies for enhancing muscular adaptations over an 8-week training cycle
claim: Progressing by adding repetitions at a fixed load and progressing by adding load at fixed repetitions gave similar hypertrophy and strength over 8 weeks, which supports double progression.
population: 43 resistance-trained adults, lower-body exercises, twice weekly

quote: A consensus definition is proposed: "Deloading is a period of reduced training stress designed to mitigate physiological and psychological fatigue, promote recovery, and enhance preparedness for subsequent training."
claim: Deloading is a period of reduced training stress meant to reduce physical and mental fatigue, promote recovery and prepare for the next training block.
population: expert strength and physique coaches (Delphi, n = 21-34)
caveat: expert consensus, not outcome evidence

quote: This would be achieved through a decrease in either the number of sets per training session, the number of repetitions per set, or through a reduction in training frequency. ... Deloading could be pre-planned and organized around the athlete’s lifestyle or integrated using an autoregulatory approach.
claim: Coaches agreed that a deload reduces volume by cutting sets per session, repetitions per set or training days, and that deloads can be pre-planned or autoregulated.
used_for: how to build a deload week
caveat: expert consensus; no trial has compared deload designs

quote: The typical duration of a deload was 6.4 ± 1.7 days, integrated into the training programme every 5.6 ± 2.3 weeks. ... training volume would decrease (through a reduction in both repetitions per set and sets per week), but training frequency would remain unchanged during deloads.
claim: Competitive strength and physique athletes typically deload for about 6 days every 5-6 weeks, cutting sets and repetitions while keeping training frequency unchanged.
caveat: describes practice, not effectiveness; recreational lifters may need deloads less often

quote: our findings suggest that a 1-week deload period at the midpoint of a 9-week RT program appears to negatively influence measures of lower body muscle strength but has no effect on lower body hypertrophy, power or local muscular endurance.
claim: In trained young adults, a 1-week complete break from training in the middle of a 9-week program reduced lower-body strength gains compared with continuous training and did not change hypertrophy.
used_for: full rest week versus reduced-load deload
caveat: the deload was complete cessation, not reduced training; a single study

quote: Results of the meta-analyses comparing NP and periodized training demonstrated an overall effect on 1RM strength favoring periodized training (ES 0.31, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.04, 0.57]; Z = 2.28, P = 0.02). In contrast, muscle hypertrophy did not differ between NP and periodized training
claim: In volume-equated studies, periodized training gave a small advantage for 1RM strength over non-periodized training (effect size 0.31) but no difference in hypertrophy.

quote: Subgroup analyses indicated an effect on 1RM favoring UP in trained participants (ES 0.61, 95% CI [0.00, 1.22]; Z = 1.97 (P = 0.05)), whereas changes in 1RM did not differ between LP and UP in untrained participants
claim: Undulating periodization beat linear periodization for 1RM in trained participants (effect size 0.61, lower confidence limit 0.00) but not in untrained participants.
population: volume-equated studies; trained versus untrained subgroups
used_for: linear versus undulating models for trained lifters
caveat: borderline significance

quote: No significant differences between autoregulated and standardized load prescription were demonstrated for 1RM strength (MD = 2.07, 95% CI - 0.32 to 4.46 kg, p = 0.09, SMD = 0.21).
claim: Autoregulated load prescription (RIR-based RPE or velocity) and fixed percentage-based loading produced similar 1RM gains (non-significant 2.07 kg difference favouring autoregulation).

quote: - 0.06 (95% confidence interval [CI] - 0.20 to 0.09; p = 0.446), - 0.28 (95% CI - 0.48 to - 0.08; p = 0.007), and - 0.01 (95% CI - 0.16 to 0.18; p = 0.919) for maximal strength, explosive strength, and muscle hypertrophy, respectively. Attenuation of explosive strength was more pronounced when concurrent training was performed within the same session (p = 0.043) than when sessions were separated by at least 3 h
claim: Adding aerobic training to strength training did not reduce maximal strength or hypertrophy gains, but slightly reduced explosive strength gains (SMD -0.28), mainly when both were done in the same session rather than at least 3 h apart.
used_for: scheduling lifting for runners, cyclists and climbers
caveat: highly trained endurance or strength athletes are underrepresented; Huiberts2024 found small lower-body strength interference in men

quote: Concurrent training showed blunted lower-body strength adaptations in males, but not in females (male: - 0.43, 95% confidence interval [- 0.64 to - 0.22], female: 0.08 [- 0.34 to 0.49], group difference: P = 0.03).
claim: Concurrent strength and endurance training blunted lower-body strength gains in men (SMD -0.43) but not in women (SMD 0.08) compared with strength training alone.
population: healthy adults aged 18-50 y, 59 studies, 1346 participants
used_for: expectations for lower-body strength in male endurance athletes who lift
caveat: small effect; data on hypertrophy were insufficient

quote: Push-up exercise with similar load to 40%1RM bench press is comparably effective for muscle hypertrophy and strength gain over an 8-week training period.
claim: Push-ups loaded to about 40% of bench-press 1RM produced similar chest and triceps hypertrophy and bench-press strength gains as bench pressing at 40% 1RM over 8 weeks.
caveat: small single study in untrained men

quote: A dose-response relationship illustrated greater performance deficits with ≥60 s (-4.6%) than with <60 s (-1.1%) SS per muscle group.
claim: Static stretching of 60 s or more per muscle group before activity reduced performance by about 4.6%, while less than 60 s reduced it by only about 1.1%.
used_for: static stretching dose in a warm-up
caveat: testing was 3-5 min after stretching, mostly without dynamic activity afterwards

quote: All forms of training induced ROM improvements, typically lasting <30 min. ... stretching within a warm-up that includes additional poststretching dynamic activity is recommended for reducing muscle injuries and increasing joint ROM with inconsequential effects on subsequent athletic performance.
claim: Acute range-of-motion gains from stretching typically last less than 30 min; stretching inside a warm-up followed by dynamic activity is recommended and has inconsequential effects on performance.
used_for: where to place stretching in a session
caveat: the same review found no clear effect of static or PNF stretching on all-cause or overuse injuries; injury prevention belongs to MON

quote: Resistance training increased range of motion (effect size [ES] = 0.73; p < 0.001) with the exception of no significant range of motion improvement with resistance training using only body mass. There were no significant differences between resistance training versus stretch training (ES = 0.08; p = 0.79)
claim: Resistance training with external load increased range of motion (effect size 0.73) about as much as stretching (difference 0.08, not significant); training with body mass only did not significantly improve range of motion.
caveat: untrained and sedentary people improved more than trained people

quote: Static stretching improves flexibility in adults, with no additional benefit observed beyond 4 min per session or 10 min per week.
claim: Static stretching improves flexibility, with no additional benefit beyond about 4 min of cumulative stretching per session or 10 min per week.
number: 4 min per session; 10 min per week
caveat: people with poor baseline flexibility improved more; intensity and frequency did not matter

quote: Warm-up was shown to improve performance in 79% of the criterions examined.
claim: Warming up (with activities other than stretching alone) improved performance in 79% of the outcomes examined, with little evidence of harm.
caveat: search ended 2008; few well-conducted RCTs

quote: Full ROM training produced significantly greater adaptations than partial ROM on muscle strength (ES = 0.56, p = 0.004) and lower-limb hypertrophy (ES = 0.88, p = 0.027).
claim: Full range-of-motion training produced greater strength (effect size 0.56) and lower-limb hypertrophy (effect size 0.88) than partial range-of-motion training.
used_for: cost of reducing range of motion when a joint is irritated
caveat: partial range at long muscle lengths may be an exception (lengthened partials)

quote: In Fig. 2, estimates at 90% and 70% 1RM are ~ 5 and ~ 15 repetitions, respectively. ... at 80% 1RM, the estimate for the SD about the point estimate is 2.51 repetitions, whereas at 60% 1RM the estimate is 4.36 repetitions.
claim: On average people complete about 5 repetitions at 90% 1RM and about 15 at 70% 1RM, but individuals vary widely (SD about 2.5 repetitions at 80% and about 4.4 at 60%), so percentage-to-repetition tables and repetition-based 1RM estimates are rough.
number: ~5 reps at 90%; ~15 reps at 70%; SD 2.51 at 80%; SD 4.36 at 60%
population: 7289 individuals from 269 studies, mostly healthy trained men
caveat: leg press allows more repetitions (about 13 at 80%); use RIR to fine-tune loads

quote: Deloading was undertaken using a proactive, pre-planned strategy (or in combination with an autoregulated approach) and undertaken when performance stalled or during periods of increased muscle soreness or joint aches.
claim: Strength and physique athletes deload on a pre-planned schedule, often combined with autoregulation, and also when performance stalls or muscle soreness or joint aches increase.
caveat: describes practice, not effectiveness

quote: we advise restricting the warm-up to exercise-specific warm-ups, and only prioritize stretching if the goal of training is to increase flexibility.
claim: For time-efficient strength training, limit the warm-up to exercise-specific warm-up sets and include stretching only when improving flexibility is a goal.
used_for: warm-up design when time is short
caveat: expert opinion

quote: Strength and muscle size (at least in younger populations) can be maintained for up to 32 weeks with as little as 1 session of strength training per week and 1 set per exercise, as long as exercise intensity (relative load) is maintained
claim: In younger people, strength and muscle size can be maintained for up to 32 weeks with as little as 1 strength session per week and 1 set per exercise, provided the relative load (intensity) stays the same.
number: up to 32 weeks; 1 session per week; 1 set per exercise
population: general populations, mostly younger adults (narrative review)
caveat: narrative review; insufficient data for athletes or military personnel

quote: in older populations, maintaining muscle size may require up to 2 sessions per week and 2-3 sets per exercise, while maintaining exercise intensity
claim: In older people, maintaining muscle size may need up to 2 strength sessions per week and 2-3 sets per exercise, with intensity kept the same.
number: up to 2 sessions per week; 2-3 sets per exercise

quote: reducing training volume and frequency at the midpoint and endpoint of an 8-week resistance training program does not appear to hinder adaptations in muscle hypertrophy and strength-endurance in untrained young men
claim: In untrained young men, building short deload weeks (reduced volume and frequency) into an 8-week resistance program did not impair gains in muscle thickness or strength-endurance compared with continuous training.
population: 19 untrained young men, within-subject design (leg extension and biceps curl only)
caveat: small sample, only 8 weeks, untrained men; shows a deload did no harm, not that it helps

quote: In the deload condition, a similar training program was followed; however, during weeks 4 and 8, the exercises were performed only once per week with 2 sets per exercise.
claim: The deload tested in this trial was weeks 4 and 8 with each exercise trained only once per week for 2 sets, instead of twice per week for 6-8 sets.
number: weeks 4 and 8; once per week; 2 sets per exercise

quote: Muscle growth appears to be more pronounced when resistance exercise is progressively overloaded. Notably, training without overload progression is sufficient to induce muscle hypertrophy in young, untrained women.
claim: In untrained young women, progressive overload produced more triceps growth than training with a fixed load, but training without any load progression still produced hypertrophy.
population: 55 untrained young women, one arm exercise, 8 weeks
caveat: the authors state that longer-term effects of non-progressive training are unknown

quote: ∑TB increased in both training conditions compared with Control, with greater increases in PO relative to N-PO (PO = 0.79 cm, +22.9% > N-PO = 0.41 cm, +11.6% > Control = 0.05 cm, +1.8%; P < 0.001)
claim: Summed triceps muscle thickness rose by about 22.9% with progressive overload and about 11.6% with a fixed load, against 1.8% in the non-exercising control arm.
population: 55 untrained young women, triceps extension 3 x 8-12, 3 days per week, 8 weeks
caveat: one muscle, one exercise, ultrasound thickness

quote: Compared with RT, CT significantly improved aerobic capacity (SMD 0.77; p = 0.02), while strength, power, and hypertrophy outcomes were comparable.
claim: In an umbrella review, combining resistance and endurance training improved aerobic capacity compared with resistance training alone (SMD 0.77) while strength, power and hypertrophy outcomes were comparable.
population: healthy, mostly recreationally trained people (17 meta-analyses, 1492 participants)
caveat: data from highly trained and elite athletes are scarce

quote: No significant effects of training sequence were found; however, trends suggest performing RT before ET may favor strength (SMD 1.69; p < 0.001) and hypertrophy (SMD 0.83; p = 0.36) gains.
claim: Training order (resistance before endurance or the reverse) showed no significant effect overall, but trends favoured resistance before endurance for strength (SMD 1.69) and, non-significantly, for hypertrophy (SMD 0.83).
caveat: the sequence statement is a trend, not a confirmed effect; the hypertrophy result was not significant

quote: Both muscle thickness and unilateral lat pulldown 10-repetition-maximum improvements were similar between the two conditions.
claim: In resistance-trained adults, lengthened partial repetitions and full range-of-motion repetitions gave similar gains in elbow flexor and extensor thickness and in lat-pulldown strength-endurance over an upper-body program.
population: 30 resistance-trained adults, upper body only, 2 sessions per week for 8 weeks
caveat: upper body only; partial range was performed in the lengthened position

quote: Trainees seeking to maximize muscle size should likely emphasize the stretched position, either by using a full ROM or LPs during upper-body resistance training.
claim: To maximise muscle size in upper-body training, the stretched (lengthened) position should be emphasised, either with full range of motion or with lengthened partial repetitions.

quote: Eleven studies were included in the review. Full ROM and pROM performed in the initial part of the ROM elicited greater muscle hypertrophy of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, biceps brachii, and brachialis distal sites (between-groups ES: 0.20-0.90) than pROM performed in the final part of the ROM.
claim: In a systematic review of eleven studies, full range of motion and partial range of motion in the initial part of the movement produced more hypertrophy of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis and biceps than partial range in the final part (effect sizes 0.20-0.90).
population: healthy adults in range-of-motion hypertrophy trials
caveat: few studies, several muscles; some muscles showed other patterns (for example middle-range partials favoured the triceps)

quote: Higher-load (>80% of single repetition maximum) prescriptions maximised strength gains, and all prescriptions comparably promoted muscle hypertrophy.
claim: In healthy adults, loads above 80% of 1RM gave the largest strength gains, while all resistance-training prescriptions in the network (different loads, sets, frequencies) promoted hypertrophy about equally.
population: healthy adults, 178 strength and 119 hypertrophy randomised trials

quote: higher-load, multiset, thrice-weekly training (standardised mean difference (95% credible interval); 1.60 (1.38 to 1.82) vs CTRL) was the highest-ranked RTx for strength, and higher-load, multiset, twice-weekly training (0.66 (0.47 to 0.85) vs CTRL) was the highest-ranked RTx for hypertrophy.
claim: The highest-ranked prescription was higher-load, multiple-set training 3 times per week for strength (SMD 1.60 versus no exercise) and higher-load, multiple-set training twice per week for hypertrophy (SMD 0.66); many prescriptions had similar effects.
caveat: ranking is not proof that the top prescription is clearly better than neighbouring ones

quote: "Weekend Warrior" and single-set resistance exercise are the approaches most strongly supported by current research, while snacking and eccentric minimal doses are emerging concepts with promising results.
claim: Among minimal-dose strategies for people not yet doing resistance exercise, one weekly session ("Weekend Warrior") and single-set training are the best supported; short exercise "snacks" and low-volume eccentric work are promising but newer.
population: people not currently engaged in resistance exercise (narrative overview)
caveat: narrative overview; strength outcomes only

quote: "Weekend Warrior," which minimizes training frequency, is resistance exercise performed in one weekly session.
claim: A single weekly resistance session is a defined minimal-dose strategy that increases strength in people who are not training.
population: people not currently engaged in resistance exercise

quote: Both VBT and PBT can enhance strength, jump, linear sprint and CODs performance effectively without significant group difference.
claim: In a small meta-analysis, velocity-based training and percentage-of-1RM training both improved strength, jump, sprint and change-of-direction performance with no significant difference between them.
caveat: very small meta-analysis

quote: The overall effect size was SMD=0.26 (95%CL 0.03 to 0.49, P=0.03, I²=0).
claim: A second meta-analysis found a small advantage of velocity-based over percentage-based training for maximal strength (SMD 0.26, lower confidence limit 0.03), larger in athletes than in non-athletes.
caveat: small effect and wide uncertainty; contradicts the null result of the other VBT meta-analysis

quote: the magnitude of improvement in 1RM following periodized resistance training was greater than non-periodized resistance training (ES = 0.43, 95% CI 0.27-0.58; P < 0.001)
claim: A meta-analysis of 18 studies found periodized resistance training raised 1RM more than non-periodized training (effect size 0.43), with undulating models and untrained participants showing larger gains.
caveat: older studies, not all volume-matched

quote: While inclusion of some type of exercises in the warm-up may reduce long-term injury risk, as in other periods of the training session, there is no support for acute injury protection.
claim: An international expert panel agreed that a warm-up may lower long-term injury risk like other parts of a session but gives no support for acute injury protection.

quote: Experts identified a 3-layer model comprising general and specific exercises and conditioning activities, with the latter being voluntary contractions of sufficient volume and intensity to induce postactivation performance enhancement.
claim: The expert panel described a warm-up as three layers: general exercise, specific exercise, and optional conditioning activities (voluntary contractions heavy enough to enhance performance).
